clips.title: tj-actions Supply Chain Attack – How to Check & Fix It NOW
clips.why: A security company explains the attack from the story a few days after it happened, and what affected teams had to do.
look: What happened to an action used in more than 23,000 repositories.
Which secrets were at risk: AWS keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens and private keys.
How to check whether a repo was affected, and the first steps to take.
clips.after: fcp's workflows already write the full SHA with a version comment, which is exactly the line that would have kept this attack out.

clips.title: GitHub Actions Policy Update: Blocking & SHA Pinning Explained!
clips.why: Mickey Gousset shows the setting that makes an organization refuse any action that is not pinned by full SHA.
look: The policy option GitHub added in August 2025 that requires every action to be pinned by its full SHA.
That an organization can enforce pinning for every repo at once.
A question to think about while you watch: why is a rule in the settings stronger than asking every workflow author to remember?
clips.after: zizmor's unpinned-uses check, which you run in the lab, finds the same lines before they ever reach GitHub.

clips.title: GitHub Actions Reusable Workflows FULL TUTORIAL with Examples: Templates on Steroids
clips.why: A complete walk through writing a reusable workflow and calling it, with inputs and secrets.
look: on: workflow_call and the typed inputs, like the props of a component.
How the caller passes inputs under with: and secrets by name.
The caller's uses: line that points at the file, and the @ref after it.
clips.after: fcp calls Byte's review workflow exactly this way, with the @ref being a full commit SHA instead of a branch.

practice.q: Which of these lines is pinned?

options.why: A tag with a full version number is still a tag, and tags can be moved.
A short hash can match more than one commit, and an attacker can create a matching one on purpose. Use all 40 characters.
The full SHA names fixed content, and the comment keeps the version readable for people.

practice.q: Finish the command that prints the commit a version tag points at today.
practice.hint: The field of the commit object that holds the 40-character hash.
practice.why: The commits endpoint accepts a tag name and answers with that commit; .sha picks out the hash you pin.

practice.q: Finish the on: block of a workflow that only other workflows may start.
practice.after:
:
    inputs:
      name:
        required: true
        type: string
practice.hint: It is the event that means 'another workflow calls me'.
practice.why: workflow_call turns a file into a reusable workflow with typed inputs, which callers start with a uses: line.

practice.q: A reusable workflow needs the secret NPM_TOKEN. The caller passes nothing under secrets:. What does the called workflow see?

options.text: The secret, because both workflows run in the same organization
options.why: Secrets never flow by themselves. The caller must hand each one over.

options.text: An empty value, because the caller did not pass it by name or with secrets: inherit
options.why: Only the secrets the caller names (or all of them with secrets: inherit) reach the called workflow.

options.text: The secret, but only if the reusable workflow lives in the same repo
options.why: Same repo or not, the called workflow only gets the secrets its caller passes.

practice.q: Put the steps of pinning a container image in order.
items: Pull the tag you want, for example docker pull node:24-bookworm-slim
Print the digest with docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
Write container: node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:<digest> in the job
Run the job: it uses exactly that image until someone moves the pin in a reviewed PR
practice.why: The digest only exists for an image you have, so you pull first, then read the digest, then write it into the workflow. After that, rebuilding the tag changes nothing for you.

practice.q: Why does the independent-approval check run from an image instead of from code checked out of fcp?

options.text: Images start faster than a checkout
options.why: Speed is not the reason. The reason is who can change the program that decides.

options.text: A pull request in fcp could edit code that lives in fcp, including the check that judges it
options.why: With the program in a pinned image from another repo, the PR being judged cannot change the judge, and fcp needs no token to read the platform repo.

options.text: GitHub does not allow required checks to run from a checkout
options.why: Many required checks run from a checkout. This is our design choice, not a GitHub rule.
